lesson.title: Approaching Infinity from Just One Side
lesson.summary: Some functions blow up toward positive or negative infinity depending on which direction you approach from, and learning to read that difference is the key to understanding vertical asymptotes.
lesson.body:
Recall that a one-sided limit asks what happens to f(x) as x approaches a number a from only the left (x approaching a from below) or only the right (x approaching a from above), without requiring the two directions to agree. An infinite limit describes what happens when f(x) itself grows without bound rather than settling near a finite number. A one-sided infinite limit combines both ideas: it asks whether f(x) grows without bound, toward positive infinity or negative infinity, as x approaches a from just one side.

The notation looks like lim as x approaches a from the right of f(x) equals infinity, or lim as x approaches a from the left of f(x) equals negative infinity. Writing "equals infinity" is a convention, not a claim that the limit reaches a real number. Infinity is not a value the function actually attains; the notation is shorthand for "f(x) increases without any upper bound as x gets arbitrarily close to a from that side." A limit that equals infinity in this sense still counts as a limit that does not exist in the traditional finite sense.

Consider f(x) = 1/(x-3), undefined at x=3 because the denominator becomes zero there. Approach from the right: x=3.1 gives 1/0.1=10, x=3.01 gives 1/0.01=100, x=3.001 gives 1/0.001=1000. As x nears 3 from above, the denominator is a tiny positive number, so the fraction grows without bound in the positive direction, so lim x to 3 from the right of 1/(x-3) equals infinity. Now approach from the left: x=2.9 gives 1/(-0.1) = -10, x=2.99 gives 1/(-0.01) = -100, x=2.999 gives 1/(-0.001) = -1000. Here the denominator is a tiny negative number, so the fraction grows without bound in the negative direction, so lim x to 3 from the left of 1/(x-3) equals negative infinity.

Because the left-hand and right-hand behaviors disagree, one heading toward positive infinity and the other toward negative infinity, the two-sided limit at x=3 does not exist, not even as an infinite limit. Graphically this is what a vertical asymptote at x=3 looks like: the curve rockets upward as it is traced from the right of the asymptote and plunges downward as it is traced from the left. Compare this to g(x)=1/(x-3)^2, where both one-sided limits equal positive infinity because squaring removes the sign difference, so there the two-sided limit can legitimately be reported as infinity, since both directions agree.

Not every one-sided infinite limit involves a rational function with two sides to compare. Consider f(x) = ln(x), whose domain only includes x>0, so only the right-hand limit as x approaches 0 makes sense; there is no left-hand behavior to describe at all. Checking values confirms the output falls without bound: ln(0.1) is approximately -2.303, ln(0.01) is approximately -4.605, and ln(0.001) is approximately -6.908, so lim x to 0 from the right of ln(x) equals negative infinity. This is a second common pattern for a one-sided infinite limit: not a clash between two competing one-sided behaviors, but a function whose domain restricts it to only one side of the point in the first place, so the vertical asymptote at x=0 only has a single branch to describe.

Reading one-sided infinite limits correctly is essential for sketching rational functions and for later work on end behavior, since every vertical asymptote of a rational function is really a statement about a pair of one-sided infinite limits. Whenever a denominator can equal zero, checking each side separately, rather than assuming symmetry, is the only reliable way to describe what the graph is doing near that input value.
